# The Night Shift

The radio program was called *Night Signals*, and it aired from midnight to three a.m. on a frequency so far down the dial that Marta's radio only found it if she turned the knob slowly, like she was coaxing a shy animal out from under a porch. She'd been listening for two years, ever since her husband died and sleep became something that happened to other people.

The host, who called himself only Meridian, played obscure jazz and read listener letters and sometimes, on the best nights, just talked—about the moon, about highway rest stops, about why certain songs sound better in October. Marta never called in. But she listened every night, and it felt like a secret room she could enter without leaving her house.

She discovered her neighbor listened too on a Tuesday in March, when she took her trash out at 12:40 a.m. and heard it. The same broadcast, faintly, coming from the house next door—the Hendersons' place, though old Mr. Henderson had died and his daughter had moved in last fall. The sound leaked through an open window, and Marta stood in the cold holding her trash bag lid like a shield.
